solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Tradesman's first to applaud as it's put back into service

indicators.note: the first letter to 'applaud' is its opening A
words put back run in the reverse direction

parts.note: RN = Royal Navy, the Senior Service
the two words as they stand, reversed to TISA

explanation.surface: A craftsman's work is clapped as a machine is returned to working order.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s on Tradesman is 'is', which then reads with 'put back into': AS IT is put back into RN. The Royal Navy is the Senior Service, so 'service' gives RN.
explanation.definitionFit: An artisan is a skilled manual worker, a tradesman.

clue.text: City like to restrict United, and can

parts.note: as = like, as in 'dressed as a clown'
U = United, as in football team names

explanation.surface: A fan of a football club talks of hemming in United, with a drink can in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' is the word AS, not a verb; U for United comes from team names like Man U.
explanation.definitionFit: Austin is the state capital of Texas.

clue.text: Malign suggestion conveys a bit less than expected

indicators.note: DUE falls a bit short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a trace is a slight suggestion, as in 'a trace of irony'
expected = DUE, cut short by one letter

explanation.surface: A snide hint implies that someone earned rather less than they were meant to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Malign' reads as an adjective with 'suggestion'; it is the verb, to speak ill of, which is what traduce means.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to speak falsely and damagingly of someone.

clue.text: Handsome older man lives for high times

indicators.note: high means intoxicated, so the letters of LIVES FOR are all over the place

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'

explanation.surface: A dashing older man is said to live for the good life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High times' looks like a phrase for fun; 'high' is the anagram signal and 'times' is the X of multiplication.
explanation.definitionFit: A silver fox is an attractive grey-haired older man.

clue.text: Yes, end war somehow, with a conclusion to hostility when resolutions come into effect?

indicators.note: the conclusion to hostility is its final letter
somehow says the letters come together in some unstated way

parts.note: A is used as is, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: A peace treaty is signed, ending hostility, just as new resolutions take effect.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends the resolutions are diplomatic ones settling a war; the definition wants the promises people make on 1 January.
explanation.definitionFit: New Year resolutions are meant to start on 1 January; the question mark flags the playful definition.

clue.text: County embraces introduction of treatment with universal medication

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its first letter

parts.note: Lincs is the short form of Lincolnshire, an English county
U = universal, the film classification for all ages

explanation.surface: A county council starts a treatment programme with medicine for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincs, short for Lincolnshire, is an English county. Here 'with' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Linctus is a syrupy cough medicine.

clue.text: Violent robbery topped former convict

indicators.note: a topped word loses its head, the first letter in a down clue

parts.note: BLAG, slang for a violent robbery, loses its B

explanation.surface: A former prisoner was involved in a violent raid.
explanation.walkthrough: Blag is British criminal slang for a robbery with violence; an old lag is a habitual or former convict.
explanation.definitionFit: A lag, usually 'old lag', is British slang for a former prisoner.

clue.text: Stylish tailcoat — nothing on the inside, no pockets

indicators.note: with nothing inside, tailcoat keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: TAILCOAT emptied leaves its outer letters T…T

explanation.surface: A tailor describes a smart tailcoat cut without any pockets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No pockets' reads as a feature of the coat, but 'no' is a letter source and 'pockets' the instruction to put something inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Natty means smart and stylish in dress.

clue.text: Port is comparatively piquant

definitions.meaning: a port city on the Moroccan side of the Strait of Gibraltar

explanation.surface: A wine note: port is sharper in taste than the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' reads as the fortified wine, which fits 'piquant'; it is the Moroccan city of Tangier, and 'comparatively' asks for the -ER form of tangy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangier is a port on the Strait of Gibraltar, and tangier is the comparative of tangy.

clue.text: Husband unhappy with friends turning up last-minute

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A husband is miserable because his friends arrive at the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' looks like friends arriving; it is the reversal of the whole string H SAD PALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Last-minute work is rushed and careless, which is slapdash.

clue.text: Rogue Conservative friend invested in stolen goods

indicators.note: to be invested in is to be put inside

explanation.surface: A crooked Tory politician's pal has put money into stolen property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested in' reads as a money term; here it only means placed inside SWAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both playful words for a mischievous rascal rather than a real villain.

clue.text: Country's head of agriculture got back around noon

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
GOT back reads it from right to left

parts.note: the word as it stands, reversed to TOG
N = noon, the abbreviation used in times

explanation.surface: A nation's farming minister returned home at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s is 'has', joining the definition: TOG around N, and the head of agriculture's A follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is a Polynesian kingdom in the South Pacific.

clue.text: One sister has run away to get engaged

parts.note: a sister is a senior nurse in a British hospital
R = run in cricket scoring; this letter leaves NURSE

explanation.surface: A nun or sibling elopes in order to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run away to get engaged' is an elopement; 'engaged' means busy, as a phone line or toilet is. In British hospitals a sister is a senior nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: Engaged here is the busy sense used of a phone line or a toilet door, not betrothed.

clue.text: One arrives in good time — European travelling by rail and road

indicators.note: travelling letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: A European commuter who goes by train and car always turns up on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Road' shrinks to its abbreviation RD before joining BY RAIL in the anagram; 'and' just adds it.
explanation.definitionFit: From the proverb 'the early bird catches the worm': the phrase names anyone who turns up ahead of time.

clue.text: Ignoring temperature, desperate to support engineers — I'm compensating

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting word sits below

parts.note: bursting = desperate, as in 'bursting to tell'
T = temperature; this letter leaves BURSTING

explanation.surface: An engineer, eager to help but ignoring the heat, is paying people back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm' sits at the end of the clue, looking attached to the definition, but it is wordplay. RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps; 'desperate' is bursting, as in bursting to go.
explanation.definitionFit: To reimburse is to compensate someone for money spent.

clue.text: Things such as drama roles encapsulating revolutionary from Niger

indicators.note: revolutionary letters turn over into a new order

parts.note: parts are roles in a play

explanation.surface: Acting parts are given to a rebel from the African country of Niger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary from Niger' reads as a rebel; 'revolutionary' is the anagram signal and 'from Niger' its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: drama is one of the arts presented on stage, alongside dance and music.

clue.text: Ultimately, crushing defeat ended in whitewash

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter

explanation.surface: A crushing defeat finished with the team losing without scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whitewash' is a sports term for a total rout, which fits the surface; the definition wants its sense of covering up faults.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitewash in its figurative sense is covering up faults, the same idiom as passing over them lightly.

clue.text: Observe fewer things without flaws

parts.note: less = fewer, of a quantity of things

explanation.surface: An inspector notices fewer items that are without defects.
explanation.walkthrough: The split falls after 'things': 'without flaws' is the definition, not 'things without flaws'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotless means perfectly clean, without a flaw.

clue.text: On bed, I explored being kinky — she's very fair

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman confesses to some bedroom experimentation, and her partner is very pale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' reads as just, of a lover; here it is hair colour. A peroxide blonde's hair is bleached with hydrogen peroxide.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairness is hair colour: hydrogen peroxide bleaches hair to a very pale shade.

clue.text: Unrestrained tirade about a person occupying seat

parts.note: an MP holds a seat in Parliament

explanation.surface: Someone launches into an uncontrolled tirade about a fellow passenger taking a seat.
explanation.walkthrough: The seat is a parliamentary one, so the person occupying it is an MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampant means unrestrained, flourishing unchecked.

clue.text: Operating during the day, vessel is brought in by radio control

parts.note: the dial is the tuning control on a radio

explanation.surface: A ship working by daylight is guided into port by radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' reads as a ship being brought into harbour; it is an URN, and the radio control is a tuning DIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A zoologist's term, from Latin diurnus, daily; its opposite is nocturnal.

clue.text: Climber eating hard, out-of-date bread

parts.note: the pea plant climbs with tendrils
set = hardened, as of jelly or concrete

explanation.surface: A mountaineer is chewing on hard, stale bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, and 'out-of-date' means withdrawn currency, not stale food.
explanation.definitionFit: The peseta was Spain's currency until the euro replaced it; bread is slang for money.

clue.text: Literary character's motto central to storyline in book, right?

indicators.note: the letter central to storyline is its middle one

parts.note: a tome is a large book
a saw is a proverb or saying

explanation.surface: A reader asks whether a character's catchphrase sums up the plot of the novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s is 'is', linking the definition; 'motto' is an old SAW, not a slogan. Storyline has nine letters, so its fifth, Y, is central.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Sawyer is the boy hero of Mark Twain's novel.

clue.text: A third of biscuit, absorbed by beverage, is lost

explanation.surface: A soggy biscuit, dunked in tea, falls apart and disappears into the cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A third of' looks like a fraction; A is the first letter of the answer and 'third of biscuit' is its third letter, S.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship out of sight of land has no bearings, so the idiom extends to anyone bewildered.

clue.text: Sea foam close to outcrop, birds circling around

parts.note: emus are birds, reversed to SUME

indicators.note: the letter close to the end of outcrop is its last

explanation.surface: Foam gathers by a rocky outcrop as seabirds wheel overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: The seabirds of the surface are EMUS, flightless birds that could hardly circle anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary word from Latin spuma, foam, used of the froth whipped off waves.

clue.text: Non-commissioned officer cut back tests

explanation.surface: A sergeant was reduced in rank after failing tests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut back' reads as one phrase meaning reduced; 'cut' is AXE and 'back' reverses the whole of SM AXE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: school or university examinations are formal tests.

clue.text: Welshman tucked into good food — beef

parts.note: Evan is a typical Welsh man's name

explanation.surface: A Welshman eagerly tucks into a good meal of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' is on the menu in the surface; it is also slang for a complaint. 'Tucked into' is eating in the surface and insertion in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is informal slang for a complaint, as in 'what's your beef?'.

clue.text: My hotel's out of butter

parts.note: ghee is clarified butter used in South Asian cooking
H = hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet; this letter leaves GHEE

explanation.surface: A guest complains that their hotel has run out of butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive; it is the exclamation 'My!', which GEE also is.
explanation.definitionFit: Gee and my are both mild exclamations of surprise.

clue.text: Model had to accept university place

parts.note: to sit for a portrait is to model

explanation.surface: A model had to take a place at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' reads as 'was obliged'; it is ATE, as in having a meal. 'Place' is the verb, to put somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to put something in a particular position.

clue.text: Pass artist cuddling sick animal

parts.note: to go is to pass, as a turn in a game

explanation.surface: A painter hugs a poorly pet as it passes away.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a Royal Academician, is the standard artist; 'Pass' is GO, your turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the largest of the great apes is simply an animal.
